item.title: Asymmetric Complexity and the Limits of Engine Evaluation
item.description:
Exeter College Summer Programme, University of Oxford. Mathematical Modelling, Prof. Tom Crawford. August 2026.

Chess engines report who is better under perfect play, but humans aren’t perfect players. This project models how engine evaluation and asymmetric complexity (how much harder a position is for one side than the other) evolve together.

A linear model,

has a saddle at the origin whose separatrix marks off regions where the engine favors one side but complexity carries the game to the other side’s win. A non-linear extension bounds evaluation and complexity, adds finite win states, and shows a saddle-node bifurcation as advantage begins to generate complexity. The result motivates a more human evaluation metric for broadcasting and chess education.

Methods: linear and non-linear ODEs, phase-plane analysis, bifurcation analysis, Python (NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib).

item.title: AI Should Not Be Called Human-Like: An Approach From Conceptual Engineering
item.description:
Exeter College Summer Programme, University of Oxford. Ethics of AI, Prof. Christoph Kelp and Prof. Mona Simion. August 2026.

Debates about AI existential risk usually focus on human disempowerment. This paper proposes another kind of existential risk, the self-understanding problem: AI may change what it means to be human.

Using conceptual engineering, it argues two things. First, claims that AI has human-like features (consciousness, cognition, agency) cannot be justified by theories built through anthropocentric abstraction, since those theories can’t non-circularly ground the human standard they rely on. Second, likeness claims made by trusted experts can transfer understanding in both directions, so observations of AI begin to reshape our concept of the human. The paper recommends discussing AI’s features on their own terms and answers two objections.

item.title: Beyond Morality: Nietzsche’s Non-Prescriptive Project
item.description:
Directed Studies, Historical and Political Thought, Prof. Christopher McGowan, Spring 2026

Argues that the Genealogy of Morals calls morality itself into question rather than prescribing master morality, reading Nietzsche’s perspectivism as a method that ends in productive uncertainty.

item.title: Aesthetic Transcendence: Tolstoy’s Meaning Beyond Particularity
item.description:
Directed Studies, Literature, Prof. Serena Bassi, Spring 2026

Reads the thistle of Hadji Murat’s prologue against the hero’s death to show how Tolstoy’s aesthetics carry the historical story beyond its particulars toward a meaning death cannot confine.

item.title: Questioning Hegel: Master-Slave Dialectic in Motion
item.description:
Directed Studies, Philosophy, Prof. Tamar Gendler, Spring 2026

Reconstructs Hegel’s account of self-consciousness through recognition and asks why the master-slave dialectic stops where it does, and whether the slave’s independence through labor contradicts it.

item.title: Theatricality of Imperial Rome: Counterproductive Persecution of Free Speech
item.description:
Directed Studies, Historical and Political Thought, Prof. Daniel Schillinger, Fall 2025

Traces through Tacitus’ Annals how Tiberius and Nero turned Roman politics into theater, and argues that persecuting free speech only raised its value.

item.title: Sit in Silence
item.description:
Guest column, Yale Daily News, October 2025.

We fill every idle moment with distraction, and in doing so we silence the questions that boredom would otherwise raise, questions that lead to self-knowledge.

item.title: Making Decisions Beyond the Chess Board
item.description:
TEDxColegio Nueva Granada, Bogotá, March 2025.

Every decision framework breaks down under complexity: consequences are unpredictable, intentions are self-serving, and rules are rigid. Drawing on chess, this talk argues that learning to navigate uncertainty is what actually decides outcomes.
